title: Hook a TERTIAL desk lamp's loose upper-arm spring back onto its stud so the head holds itself up
instruction: The desk lamp's head has sunk onto the desk. Make the lamp hold its head up by itself again.
context: IKEA's TERTIAL clamp lamp, sold since 1998, comes with its two upper-arm springs loose in the box. The owner hooks them on by hand (assembly sheet AA-2550118, step 3). With one spring off its stud, the other spring cannot carry the shade, so the head sinks to the desk. Owner reviews do report drooping heads, but I found no source that names a spring off its stud as the cause.
real_product:
IKEA TERTIAL work lamp. Sources:
(a) IKEA assembly instructions AA-2550118-1 (ikea.com/qa/en/assembly_instructions/tertial-work-lamp-dark-grey__AA-2550118-1-100.pdf). Page 5 lists 2 loose extension springs with loop ends. Page 9, step 3 ("2x"), shows one hand steadying the arm at the elbow while the other stretches each spring from the elbow plate's upper corner and drops its end loop over a headed stud about 42% along the upper arm. The upper arm is drawn roughly horizontal, with no special angle. Pages 7-8 give a wall-bracket option.
(b) IKEA product page (ikea.com/au/en/p/tertial-work-lamp-dark-grey-50355442): steel arm, 17 cm steel shade, ABS clamp (0-60 mm), package 56x17x12 cm and 0.92 kg, rated 4.6/5 from 2,197 reviews.
IKEA does not publish arm segment lengths or the spring rate. I inferred about 45 cm segments from the 56 cm box and the drawing; a real unit (about $20) must be measured before building.
The idea's Luxo L-1 (spec sheet: 1040 mm arm, spring-balanced; 2011 manual BRU-303-0073) has no published spring data or spring-fitting procedure. I estimate its lower-arm springs need about 60-110 N to hook on, which is beyond the YAM, and scaling them down is closed.
The real product removes the forced skill. IKEA's own drawing hooks the spring with the arm horizontal, and the force saved by the "unloading" angle is small (see skill).
fault:
One of the two upper-arm springs hangs from the elbow plate with its end loop off the stud. The remaining spring carries only about half the head's moment, so the upper arm sinks until the shade rests on the desk.
Realism caveat: I found no source showing these springs come off in use. A spares seller lists the causes of a sagging Anglepoise shade as stretched springs, a loose arm nut and heavy bulbs, not unhooked springs (relightlamps.com). The only sourced unhooked state is the assembly step, so a reviewer could see the fault as staged.
skill:
Intended skill: one gripper holds the upper arm raised toward the spring's anchor (the shortest spring path). The other stretches the spring's end loop about 3.5 cm past its free length and drops it over the stud head.

The physics check fails it. In a balanced arm the spring force is about K·d, and d only ranges from b−a to b+a (a = anchor offset from the pivot, b = stud distance from the pivot). One-spring hook-on force by arm angle, from my estimates:

| Arm angle | TERTIAL (1.6 N·m, a 3.5 cm, b 19 cm, K ≈ 120 N/m) | L-1 lower arm (7 N·m, a 4 cm, b 12 cm) |
|---|---|---|
| Best (pointing at anchor) | 18.6 N | 58 N |
| Horizontal (IKEA's drawing) | 23.2 N | 92 N |
| Drooped 40° | 25.8 N | 109 N |

For the TERTIAL, all three are within the YAM: 50 N finger effort with pad friction 1.2, and the 7 N·m wrist gives about 50 N at the TCP. With the shade resting on the desk, the arm needs no holding, so one arm can hook the spring in the drooped pose. The ordinary way works, and what remains is "stretch an elastic end onto an anchor", which is already accepted.

For the L-1, the angle matters, but even the best angle is at or past the YAM's limit. A weakened spring was rejected in #2361 and #1335.

reach_check:
Offline yam_arena.ik at real scale, station bases (0, ±0.305, 0.75), table top 0.7475. No lamp part was moved to suit the robot.

Maximum TCP height by grip:
- Top-down grip (the only kind the standard Waypoint demo supports): 0.94-0.96 m, only about 0.20 m above the desk, for x 0.15-0.40.
- 45° tilted grip: 1.04-1.18 m.
- Horizontal grip: 1.28-1.38 m.

TERTIAL layout used: clamp socket at (0.33, -0.62), 7 cm above the desk; arm plane along +y; segments 45 cm.

Lower arm leaning 55° (elbow 0.33 m above the desk):

| Upper arm angle | Stud (spring end, right arm) | Hold point 0.30 m along the arm (left arm) |
|---|---|---|
| Drooped −40° | z 0.95, needs a 30° tilt | z 0.88, 30° tilt |
| Horizontal | z 1.08, needs a 45° tilt | z 1.08, 45° tilt |
| +30° | z 1.17, needs a 60° tilt | z 1.23, horizontal grip only |
| +60° (best angle) | z 1.24, horizontal grip only | z 1.34, unreachable |

Lower arm leaning 70° (elbow 0.22 m above the desk): the stud is top-down reachable only when drooped (z 0.85). Horizontal needs a 30° tilt; +30° and +60° need 45°. The hold point needs 45° at +30° and a horizontal grip at +60°.

Verdict: the drooped "ordinary" pose is easy to reach. The unloading pose is out of top-down reach in every layout, so a demo would need a custom tilted-grip planner, as #2396 built.
reviewer_reasons:
wide-funnel deepen, 17 Nov: killed. Kill reasons, most decisive first:
1. The forced skill is not forced. A balanced-arm spring's force barely depends on arm angle: about 28% saved on a TERTIAL, and IKEA's drawing hooks it at a horizontal arm. On the TERTIAL, a one-armed hook in the drooped pose works within YAM limits. On the L-1, even the best angle needs about 60 N or more, so it is infeasible at real force, and weakening it is closed (#2361, #1335). The window where only the angle works would have to be tuned in, which is contrived.
2. Duplicates: stretching an elastic end onto an anchor against its pull is already accepted (bungee TK-MYWFKM, delta rod springs, O-ring). The holding hand puts it in the saturated hold-and-work family, and it shares the lamp family with pending #2396.
3. The fault is unsourced: no evidence that springs jump off in use, so it risks the "staged" flag. The only sourced state is a flat-pack assembly step, which is not recovery.
4. Relatability is borderline: refitting a lamp spring is occasional, not something most people do.
5. Build cost: a custom parallelogram linkage, spring slide joints with loop-on-stud capture, and a non-standard tilted-grip demo planner. Arm lengths and spring rate are unpublished, so a real unit must be bought and measured.

Not a salvage path: reframing it as TERTIAL assembly (hooking both springs while holding the arm up) has the same skill overlap.
